title: Profit, Loss, Compound Interest and Growth Rates
objectives: Compute profit as a percentage of cost (markup) and of selling price (margin), and never confuse the two bases
Combine successive discounts, markups and discounts by multiplying factors
Evaluate compound interest $A = P(1+r)^n$, compare it with simple interest, and apply the rule of 72
Compute a CAGR from start and end values over n periods and explain why it differs from the average of yearly returns
motivation: Every trading interview begins with arithmetic that looks trivial and punishes sloppy bases: is the profit margin measured on cost or on price, and did that 20% discount stack with the 10% one? These questions are not filler, markup versus margin, compounding and growth rates are the same arithmetic that pricing, financing and performance-reporting systems run all day, and this lesson makes the bases explicit so the numbers stop sliding.

blocks.text: Profit, markup and margin: one trade, two honest percentages

blocks.md: Profit is revenue minus cost, the percentage version needs a **base**. **Markup** measures profit against *cost*: $\dfrac{\text{profit}}{\text{cost}}$. **Margin** measures profit against *selling price*: $\dfrac{\text{profit}}{\text{price}}$. Buy at $80, sell at $100: profit is \$20, the markup is $\tfrac{20}{80} = 25\%$ of cost, and the margin is $\tfrac{20}{100} = 20\%$ of price. Same trade, two different numbers, both correct. When a test question says 'profit of 25%', the default convention is percent of **cost** unless it says margin or 'of the selling price'. The two are linked: a markup of $m$ on cost corresponds to a margin of $\dfrac{m}{1+m}$ on price - here $\tfrac{0.25}{1.25} = 20\%$.

The multiplier rule from the previous lesson does most of the work here. A 20% discount followed by a further 10% discount is not 30% off: it is $0.8 \times 0.9 = 0.72$ of the original price, i.e. **28% off**. The second discount applies to the already-reduced price. The same machinery runs markups and discounts in one chain: cost \$64 marked up 25% then sold at 10% off gives $64 \times 1.25 \times 0.90 = 72$, a profit of \$8 on a \$64 cost, only 12.5%, far from the 25% the markup promised. Any question that stacks changes is a single multiplication chain; write the factors, then multiply.

blocks.text: Compound interest: growth that earns on itself

blocks.caption: Principal P, rate r per period, n periods.

blocks.md: Each period multiplies the balance by $(1+r)$, so $n$ periods multiply it $n$ times: exponentiation is just repeated multiplication. Take \$2,000 at 8% for 3 years: year 1 gives $2000 \times 1.08 = 2160.00$; year 2 gives $2160 \times 1.08 = 2332.80$; year 3 gives $2332.80 \times 1.08 = 2519.42$. Simple interest would pay $2000 \times (1 + 0.08 \times 3) = 2480.00$; the extra \$39.42 is interest earned on earlier interest. For small $n$ there is a fast path: multiply by $(1+r)$ step by step and keep four decimals, it is usually quicker and safer than evaluating the power directly.

blocks.caption: \$2,000 at 8% compounded annually: \$2,160.00, then \$2,332.80, then \$2,519.42, the curve steepens because each year's base is larger.

blocks.md: Two companions round out compounding. The **rule of 72** estimates doubling time: $\dfrac{72}{r_{\%}}$ years. At 8% that is $\tfrac{72}{8} = 9$ years, and indeed $(1.08)^9 \approx 2.0$ (the exact figure is 9.006). Negative growth is the same machine with a shrink factor: a machine costing \$50,000 depreciating 20% per year is worth $50000 \times 0.8 = 40000$ after one year and $40000 \times 0.8 = 32000$ after two.

blocks.text: Growth rates over many periods: CAGR

blocks.caption: The constant annual rate that takes V_start to V_end in n years.

blocks.md: The compound annual growth rate asks: what fixed yearly rate would produce this total change? An account growing from \$80 to \$125 over 2 years has CAGR $= \sqrt{\tfrac{125}{80}} = \sqrt{1.5625} = 1.25$, i.e. **25% per year**, a clean answer because $1.25^2 = 1.5625$. CAGR smooths the path and ignores how bumpy it was, which is exactly why it disagrees with the arithmetic mean of yearly returns. A fund returning $+30\%$, then $-10\%$, then $+10\%$ has an average yearly return of $\tfrac{30 - 10 + 10}{3} = 10\%$, but compounds to $1.3 \times 0.9 \times 1.1 = 1.287$, a total gain of 28.7% and a CAGR of only about 8.8%. The gap is **volatility drag**: losses shrink the base that later gains work on.

blocks.title: Average return is not compounded return
blocks.md: The arithmetic mean of yearly returns is always at least the CAGR, with the gap growing with volatility. If a question gives yearly returns and asks 'overall growth', multiply the factors; if it asks for the 'average annual rate' of a start/end pair, take the $n$-th root. Read which one is wanted.

blocks.title: Companion practice: the Mental Math page
blocks.md: The platform's Mental Math page drills multiplier chains and percent-of-cost/percent-of-price conversions under the clock, precisely the reflexes markup-versus-margin and discount-stacking questions demand. Warm up there before any timed set.

guidedExercise.prompt: A shop buys an item for \$64 and prices it with a 25% markup on cost. The item then sells at a 10% discount off the ticket price. Compute the ticket price, the selling price, and the final profit as a percentage of cost. Was the shop's realised margin 25%?
hints: Markup on cost: multiply the cost by $1.25$.
A 10% discount is the multiplier $0.90$ applied to the ticket price.
Profit percentage of cost = (selling price, cost)/cost.
guidedExercise.solution: Ticket price $= 64 \times 1.25 = \$. Selling price $= 80 \times 0.90 = \$. Profit $= 72 - 64 = \$, so as a percentage of cost $\dfrac{8}{64} = \textbf{12.5\%}$ - not 25%. The 10% discount erased more than half of the markup's percentage, because the discount acted on the larger marked-up base ($80) while the markup acted on the smaller cost (\$64). Realised margin: $\tfrac{8}{72} \approx 11.1\%$ of the selling price.

independentExercise.prompt: A fund starts the year at \$100,000 and returns +30%, then -10%, then +10% over three consecutive years. (a) Compute the year-end values. (b) State the total percentage gain over the three years. (c) Compute the arithmetic average of the three yearly returns. (d) Compute the CAGR and explain, in one sentence, why it is below the average from (c).
hints: The arithmetic average ignores that the -10% acted on a shrunken base.
independentExercise.solution: (a) $100000 \times 1.30 = 130000$; $\times 0.90 = 117000$; $\times 1.10 = 128700$. (b) Total gain $= 28.7\%$. (c) Average yearly return $= (30 - 10 + 10)/3 = 10\%$. (d) CAGR $= (1.287)^{1/3} - 1 \approx \textbf{8.8\%}$ (check: $1.088^3 \approx 1.288$). It sits below 10% because volatility drag: the -10% year multiplied a smaller base than the +30% year did, so equal-sized percentage moves do not offset.

commonMistakes: Quoting markup when the question asked for margin: on a \$60 buy and \$75 sell, markup is $15/60 = 25\%$ but margin is $15/75 = 20\%$.
Adding successive discounts or returns instead of multiplying factors: 20% then 10% off is 28% off, not 30%.
Using simple interest arithmetic on compound questions: 3 years at 8% compounds to $1.08^3 = 1.2597$, not $1 + 3 \times 0.08 = 1.24$.
Taking the arithmetic mean of yearly returns when the question asks for overall growth or CAGR.
Forgetting the rule of 72 is an estimate: at 9% it predicts 8 years and the exact answer is 8.04, fine for multiple choice, not for accounting.
realWorldApplication: Retail pricing (markup then discount), credit cards and loans (compounding), and fund fact-sheets (CAGR versus annual returns) all run this lesson's arithmetic daily; being fluent in the bases is the difference between reading a price sheet and misunderstanding one.
quantFinanceApplication: Performance reporting is this lesson in production: a fund's cumulative return is the product of monthly factors, its CAGR is the n-th root minus one, and volatility drag explains why a strategy with a +10% average return and high variance can still lose money in compounding terms.
summary: Markup divides profit by cost; margin divides profit by selling price. A markup of m corresponds to a margin of m/(1+m).
Successive changes are chains of multipliers: 20% then 10% off is $0.8 \times 0.9 = 0.72$, i.e. 28% off.
Compound interest multiplies by $(1+r)$ each period: $A = P(1+r)^n$; the rule of 72 estimates doubling time as 72/r.
CAGR $= (V_{end}/V_{start})^{1/n} - 1$, and it is always at most the arithmetic mean of the yearly returns, the difference is volatility drag.
Negative growth uses the same machine with a factor below 1: 20% annual depreciation for two years leaves $0.8^2 = 64\%$ of the value.

quiz.prompt: An item costs \$150 and is priced with a 40% markup on cost. What is the selling price in dollars?
quiz.explanation: Markup on cost: $150 \times 1.40 = 210$. (Note: the margin on that price would be $60/210 \approx 28.6\%$, not 40%.)

quiz.prompt: A store takes 20% off a jacket, then a further 10% off the reduced price. The total discount is:
quiz.explanation: Multipliers: $0.8 \times 0.9 = 0.72$ of the original price, i.e. 28% off. The second discount applies to the already-reduced base.

quiz.prompt: \$1,000 is invested at 5% compounded annually for 2 years. What is the final balance in dollars?
quiz.explanation: $1000 \times 1.05 = 1050.00$, then $1050 \times 1.05 = 1102.50$. Simple interest would have given only 1,100.00.

quiz.prompt: A trader buys at \$60 and sells at \$75. What is the profit as a margin (a percentage of the selling price)?
quiz.explanation: Profit is \$15. As a percentage of the selling price: $15/75 = 20\%$. As a markup on cost it would be $15/60 = 25\%$, a different question.

quiz.prompt: An investment grows from \$500 to \$605 in 2 years with no interim flows. What is its CAGR, in percent, to one decimal place?
Using the rule of 72, approximately how many years does it take money to double at 9% annual growth? (Accept within half a year.)
quiz.explanation: $72/9 = 8$ years. The exact doubling time is $\ln 2 / \ln 1.09 \approx 8.04$ years, so the rule of 72 is accurate here.

flashcards.back: Markup = profit/cost; margin = profit/selling price. A markup of m equals a margin of m/(1+m). Default convention in tests: profit percent means percent of cost.
$A = P(1+r)^n$. Each period multiplies by (1+r); compare simple interest $P(1 + nr)$.
Doubling time in years is about 72 divided by the percentage rate. At 8%: 9 years; at 9%: 8 years; exact values 9.006 and 8.04.

flashcards.front: A colleague says a fund returning +30%, -10%, +10% grew 10% per year. What is wrong?
flashcards.back: That is the arithmetic mean. Compounding gives $1.3 \times 0.9 \times 1.1 = 1.287$, a CAGR of about 8.8%, volatility drag makes the mean an overestimate.
